lessons.title: Conversations that build trust
lessons.description: Listen with intention. Explain with clarity. Make every interaction matter.
steps: Start with the person
Introduce yourself and your role. Ask what matters most today, then listen without interrupting. Acknowledge the emotion before moving to the clinical agenda.
Make understanding a shared responsibility
Use plain language and small chunks of information. Ask: “To check that I explained this clearly, how will you describe the plan in your own words?” Re-explain and check again when needed.
Close the loop
Agree on the next step, who owns it, and when it will happen. Explain follow-up and locally appropriate safety-net advice. Use a qualified interpreter when needed rather than assuming understanding.
lessons.takeaway: Teach-back is a check on how clearly you explained—not a test of the patient.
lessons.question: A fictional patient has nodded through a discharge explanation. Time is limited. What most directly checks how clearly you explained the next step?
answers: Repeat the key points, then ask whether any questions remain.
Invite the patient to explain the next step in their own words.
Give a written summary, then ask them to read it after discharge.
lessons.feedback: An open teach-back prompt reveals what needs clarification without blaming the patient.
lessons.reflect: What is one phrase you could replace with clearer, more human language in your next conversation?
rationales: Repeating information can help, but does not itself reveal understanding.

Written support is useful, but does not confirm understanding before the conversation ends.

lessons.title: Small checks. Safer care.
lessons.description: Build safer habits around medications, transitions, and everyday clinical decisions.
steps: Pause before acting
Use the identifiers required by your organization. Check allergy information and the intended task against the appropriate record; location or familiarity is not a substitute for identification.
Reconcile at transitions
Compare the best available medication history with the current plan. Clarify unexplained differences with the responsible prescriber or pharmacist; do not guess. Involve the patient or caregiver.
Make uncertainty visible
If an order, dose, route, or product is unclear, pause and clarify through your local process before proceeding. Report near misses through the organizational system so the team can learn.
lessons.takeaway: A pause to resolve uncertainty is a safety action, not a delay to apologize for.
lessons.question: A fictional transfer record differs from the patient’s medication account. Both could be incomplete. What best addresses the uncertainty?
answers: Use the latest record while adding the patient’s account as a note.
Ask the patient to confirm which version they followed most recently.
Reconcile the difference with the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
lessons.feedback: Reconciliation resolves the discrepancy through the appropriate responsible team.
lessons.reflect: Where in your workflow would a deliberate pause prevent a common near miss?
rationales: A later timestamp does not resolve an unexplained discrepancy.

lessons.title: Empathy in everyday practice
lessons.description: Bring curiosity, respect, and compassion to the moments that need them most.
steps: Notice without assuming
Observe words, tone, and hesitation. Ask “What concerns you most?” rather than inferring feelings from appearance, age, culture, or diagnosis.
Acknowledge the experience
Try “That sounds like a lot to manage.” Allow silence. Validation does not require agreeing with every request or making promises outside your role.
Invite partnership
Explore the person’s priorities, practical barriers, and preferred involvement in decisions. Share options honestly, including uncertainty, and agree on an achievable next step.
lessons.takeaway: Empathy is curiosity put into words and followed by action.
lessons.question: A fictional patient says the plan is difficult. What is the most useful next response before offering a solution?
answers: Ask which part is difficult and what is getting in the way.
Offer the simplest available version of the current plan.
Explain why following the plan matters for their recovery.
lessons.feedback: Understanding the barrier allows a more useful shared response.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you made an assumption. What curious question could you ask instead? Do not include identifying details.
rationales: Understanding the barrier allows a more useful shared response.

lessons.title: A handover that gets heard
lessons.description: Use SBAR and closed-loop communication to make the next step unmistakable.
steps: Lead with situation and urgency
Identify yourself, your role, the patient using approved identifiers, and the immediate concern. State urgency clearly. Escalate emergencies immediately through local procedures.
Give relevant background and assessment
Keep background concise. Share recent changes, relevant context, and your assessment within your scope. Separate observed facts from interpretation.
Make a clear recommendation
Ask explicitly for the review or action you need and by when. Confirm the recipient’s understanding, ownership, and escalation plan if help does not arrive.
lessons.takeaway: A good handover transfers responsibility, not just information.
lessons.question: Your fictional SBAR message has been acknowledged. Which closing response best establishes a shared plan?
answers: Document that the concern was communicated to the receiving team.
Confirm the owner, agreed timing, and contingency if the plan fails.
Repeat the key findings to make sure the message was heard.
lessons.feedback: Ownership, timing, and contingency make the shared plan actionable.
lessons.reflect: Which part of your usual handover is least explicit: urgency, assessment, ownership, or next step?
rationales: Documentation matters, but does not establish what the receiving team will do.
Ownership, timing, and contingency make the shared plan actionable.

lessons.title: Infection prevention, every time
lessons.description: Turn standard precautions into consistent, situation-aware habits.
steps: Apply standard precautions to everyone
Do not wait for an infection diagnosis. Match hand hygiene, PPE, injection safety, and equipment handling to the task and anticipated exposure.
Choose protection for the exposure
Assess potential contact with blood, body fluids, mucosa, and nonintact skin. Add transmission-based precautions when indicated by local policy and current organism-specific guidance.
Protect the next interaction
Perform hand hygiene at required moments; gloves do not replace it. Remove PPE safely and clean or appropriately reprocess shared equipment before the next patient.
lessons.takeaway: Standard precautions are the starting point for every patient—not a label reserved for known infections.
lessons.question: Shared equipment looks clean and the next fictional patient has no known infection. What determines preparation for reuse?
answers: Whether the prior patient was under additional precautions.

lessons.feedback: Use the approved process and instructions; standard precautions apply to all patient care.
lessons.reflect: Which frequently touched piece of shared equipment needs a clearer cleaning handoff in your workplace?
rationales: Additional precautions can change requirements but are not the only reason to prepare equipment.

lessons.title: Think clearly under uncertainty
lessons.description: Recognize assumptions, seek disconfirming evidence, and ask for a second view.
steps: Separate observations from interpretation
State what you know, how reliable it is, and what is missing. Do not let an early label replace ongoing assessment.
Take a diagnostic pause
Ask: “What else could explain this? What does not fit? What important alternative should I not miss?” Use current, locally approved pathways and decision support within your scope.
Reassess and safety-net

Discuss uncertainty and the follow-up plan with the responsible team and patient. Specify what change warrants review and who will act on pending results. Seek senior help when concern exceeds your role or confidence.
lessons.takeaway: Confidence is useful; a clear plan for uncertainty is safer.
lessons.question: New information conflicts with the initial explanation in a fictional case. What best supports a safe reassessment?
answers: Name the mismatch and discuss alternatives with the responsible team.
Collect more observations before revisiting the explanation with anyone.
Ask a colleague whether the original explanation remains the most likely.
lessons.feedback: Making the mismatch explicit helps the team reconsider rather than anchor on an early explanation.
lessons.reflect: What question can you add to your next case discussion to challenge an early assumption?
rationales: Making the mismatch explicit helps the team reconsider rather than anchor on an early explanation.
More information can help, but should not delay communicating a significant concern.
A second opinion helps, but the question should actively invite alternatives and address the mismatch.

lessons.title: Speak up for safer teams
lessons.description: Raise concerns with clarity—and make it easier for others to do the same.
steps: Name the concern respectfully
Use observable facts and patient-focused language. TeamSTEPPS CUS can structure a concern: “I am concerned. I am uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.”
Persist through the appropriate route
If your concern is not acknowledged, repeat it clearly and escalate according to your local policy. In an emergency, activate the appropriate response without delaying for a perfect script.
Invite and thank the next voice
Leaders and colleagues can ask, “What are we missing?” Thank people who raise concerns. Debrief systems and decisions without humiliation or blame.
lessons.takeaway: Speaking up is a team skill. Receiving a concern well is the other half.
lessons.question: A junior colleague raises a concern during a busy fictional handover. What response best supports speaking up?
answers: Ask them to write down the concern for the next team meeting.
Thank them, ask what they observed, and check the concern now.
Explain the reasoning behind the current plan before discussing changes.
lessons.feedback: Acknowledgment and a timely check help the team understand and act on the concern.
lessons.reflect: How will you respond the next time someone questions your plan?
rationales: An active safety concern should be assessed rather than routinely deferred.

lessons.title: Decisions made together
lessons.description: Connect evidence and options with what matters to the individual.
steps: Make the choice visible
Invite participation and explain that there are options when a genuine choice exists. Ask how the patient wants to be involved and what matters to them.
Compare benefits, harms, and uncertainty
Use balanced, plain language and reliable decision aids. When communicating probabilities, use consistent denominators and time frames; avoid presenting relative benefit alone.
Agree, document, and revisit
Check understanding, explore preferences, and agree on a plan with the responsible clinician. Document the discussion and arrange a way to review the decision if circumstances change.
lessons.takeaway: The best available evidence and the person’s priorities belong in the same conversation.
lessons.question: Two reasonable options have different burdens for a fictional patient. What should shape the next conversation?
answers: Which option has the simplest instructions for the team to explain.
Which option most patients with similar circumstances have chosen.
The options’ trade-offs alongside the person’s priorities and needs.
lessons.feedback: Balanced evidence, uncertainty, and personal priorities belong in the same discussion.
lessons.reflect: What could you ask to uncover a priority that is not visible in the clinical record?
rationales: Simplicity matters but is only one part of a balanced discussion.

lessons.title: AI literacy, clinical responsibility
lessons.description: Use emerging tools thoughtfully. Verify outputs. Protect trust and privacy.
steps: Know the tool and its limits
Check intended use, organizational approval, and whether it has been evaluated for your setting. A fluent answer can still be wrong, incomplete, or biased.
Protect sensitive information
Do not enter patient-identifiable or confidential information into unapproved tools. Follow organizational privacy, consent, security, and data-governance requirements.
Verify before relying
Independently check clinical claims and references using authoritative, current sources. Keep qualified human oversight and follow your organization’s disclosure and documentation policies.
lessons.takeaway: A convincing output is not verified evidence. Accountability does not transfer to the tool.
lessons.question: An AI-generated summary includes a plausible claim with an unfamiliar citation. What is the strongest verification step?
answers: Locate the actual source and check whether it supports the claim.
Ask the tool to provide a more detailed explanation of its citation.
Compare the claim with a second answer from the same tool.
lessons.feedback: Independent source checking tests both the reference and the claim.
lessons.reflect: What is one clear boundary you need before using a digital or AI tool in your work?
rationales: Independent source checking tests both the reference and the claim.

lessons.title: Care for the person providing care
lessons.description: Notice strain, protect recovery, and build a practical support plan.
steps: Notice the load without judgment
Recognize changes in concentration, sleep, mood, or connection. Fatigue is not a character flaw; it can be a signal that workload and recovery need attention.
Make one feasible adjustment
Where possible, take a brief pause, meet a basic need, or ask a colleague for support. Individual habits do not replace safe staffing, rest, and organizational responsibility.
Use support early

Discuss workload and safety concerns with appropriate supervisors or occupational health. If distress persists or affects functioning, seek qualified help. For immediate danger, use local emergency support.
lessons.takeaway: Sustainable care needs both personal support and working conditions that make safe practice possible.
lessons.question: A fictional colleague reports persistent fatigue affecting concentration. What response addresses both the immediate and continuing concern?
answers: Suggest a quiet break and review how they feel at the next shift.
Offer immediate support and discuss workload through the proper route.
Share self-care resources and ask them to choose one to practise.
lessons.feedback: Immediate support and attention to working conditions address more than individual coping.
lessons.reflect: Who can you approach for practical support, and what specific request could you make?
rationales: A break may help now, but waiting can leave ongoing safety and workload concerns unaddressed.
Immediate support and attention to working conditions address more than individual coping.
Resources can help, but should not replace practical support and organizational responsibility.

lessons.title: Curiosity over assumptions
lessons.description: Recognize barriers and make room for every patient’s voice.
steps: Ask, do not presume
Ask about preferred name, language, communication needs, and what would make care more accessible. Avoid assumptions based on identity or background.
Make understanding accessible
Offer qualified interpretation and accessible formats through your service. Speak directly to the patient. Ask about hearing, vision, literacy, and practical needs sensitively.
Check the real-world plan
Explore cost, transport, support, and other barriers. Invite the patient’s preferences and work with the relevant team to adapt the plan while preserving safe care.
lessons.takeaway: Equity starts with noticing who a standard approach might leave out.
lessons.question: A fictional patient agrees to a plan, but language and access needs have not been explored. What is the best next step?
answers: Offer the standard leaflet and invite the family to explain it.
Ask whether the patient is comfortable continuing in this language.
Ask about preferred communication support and practical access needs.
lessons.feedback: A direct, respectful needs check supports an accessible and workable plan.

lessons.title: Turn reflection into better systems
lessons.description: Learn from near misses and test small, measurable changes.
steps: Describe the process, not a person to blame
Identify where the workflow becomes fragile. Involve the people who do the work and the patients affected. Use the approved incident process for safety events.
Choose a small, safe test
Define a specific aim, a measure, and a limited change to try with the appropriate approval. Check for unintended effects as well as intended benefits.
Review and adapt
Compare what happened with what you expected. Decide with the team whether to adapt, repeat, or stop the test. Share learning without identifiable patient details.
lessons.takeaway: A useful reflection ends with a small action, an owner, and a way to learn whether it helped.
lessons.question: A fictional team wants to reduce missing task owners at handover. Which next step supports learning from a small test?
answers: Agree a limited change, a measure, and a check for added burden.
Introduce an ownership field across the service and gather comments.
Repeat the handover training and count how many staff attend.
lessons.feedback: A defined test, measure, and balancing check make the result interpretable.
lessons.reflect: What small workflow improvement could your team test, and how would you know whether it helped?
rationales: A defined test, measure, and balancing check make the result interpretable.
A wider change can create avoidable disruption before a small test has generated learning.

lessons.title: Health literacy is a shared responsibility
lessons.description: Reduce jargon, information overload and the hidden effort of navigating care.
steps: Design for everyone
Understanding can change with stress, unfamiliar language and a new setting. Use clear information for everyone rather than trying to identify who appears to have low literacy.
Make the next action visible
Prioritise what the person needs to do next. Use everyday words, a short written summary and accessible formats. Ask about language and communication preferences.
Check your explanation
Use an open teach-back invitation, listen for gaps, rephrase and check again. Ask whether the plan can work with the person’s practical circumstances.
lessons.outcome: Recognise an information barrier and redesign one explanation.
lessons.takeaway: An explanation succeeds when the person can use it.

lessons.title: Make numbers mean something
lessons.description: Read absolute risk, relative change and uncertainty without being misled.
steps: Start with the denominator
Ask how many people, over what time, and with which outcome. Compare the same population, denominator and period. A count without a denominator is hard to interpret.
Show both sides of a change
In a fictional example, an outcome falls from 4 in 100 to 2 in 100. That is 2 percentage points less, and a 50% relative reduction. These describe the same change in different ways.
Check transferability
Examine the study setting, design and uncertainty. An association is not automatically a causal effect, and a result from one setting is not a forecast for another.
lessons.outcome: Explain a risk change using an absolute difference and a consistent denominator.
lessons.takeaway: Always ask: compared with what, among whom, and over how long?

lessons.title: Design around human limits
lessons.description: Recognise interruptions, memory load and fragile systems before blaming people.
steps: Look at work as it happens
Map the actual task, tools, environment, handoffs and competing demands. Ask the people doing the work where the process becomes difficult.
Build a reliable support
Reduce unnecessary complexity. Use a visible task owner, a clear cue or an approved checklist at the point of work. A reminder to concentrate is a weak response to a recurring design problem.
Test for new burden
Try a limited approved change and check its effect on errors, time and workarounds. Include people who might experience new barriers.

lessons.title: Medication lists across transitions
lessons.description: Recognise discrepancies and clarify the intended plan with the responsible team.
steps: Compare credible accounts
Use the approved reconciliation process to compare available records and the person’s account. Identify an unexplained omission, duplication or change.
Clarify, do not prescribe by inference

Communicate the verified plan

Keep the loop open until action is clear

lessons.title: Explain. Listen. Repair.
lessons.description: Practise a non-judgmental loop that reveals and repairs an explanation gap.
steps: Share one manageable idea
Use plain language, then pause. Ask about preferred language, format and interpretation support. Focus on one useful next action.
Invite the person’s explanation

cases.feedback: Teach-back checks your explanation. Rephrase in smaller chunks and support language or accessibility needs.
cases.next: The patient explains part of the plan incorrectly. What next?

cases.nextFeedback: A misunderstanding is information for the practitioner. Re-explain, check again, and involve the appropriate support rather than labeling the patient.

Trust it because there is a citation.
Ask the tool whether it is certain and accept “yes.”
cases.feedback: AI may generate inaccurate claims or nonexistent references. A citation is a starting point for checking, not proof.
cases.next: A colleague wants to paste an identifiable patient note into an unapproved public tool. What should you advise?
nextAnswers: Remove the name; that always guarantees anonymity.
Do not share the note; use only approved workflows that meet organizational privacy and governance requirements.
Proceed if the tool is free.
cases.nextFeedback: Names are not the only identifiers. Confidential clinical information needs an approved, governed workflow, not an improvised assumption of anonymity.

Pause and clarify the discrepancy with the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
Combine both lists.

hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 3: after body-fluid exposure risk. Perform hand hygiene after the task and glove removal. Use soap and water when visibly soiled and follow organism-specific and local guidance.

hygieneScenes.title: The examination is complete.
hygieneScenes.context: You have finished examining the patient and are stepping away. Pause before moving on to the wider care environment.
hygieneScenes.caption: After patient contact: protect the next interaction.
hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 4: after touching a patient. One hygiene action can meet coinciding indications; the five moments do not imply duplicate cleaning back-to-back.

hygieneScenes.title: One action can be enough.
hygieneScenes.context: You have just completed appropriate hand hygiene and go directly to the patient without touching anything else. You are about to perform the planned non-aseptic examination.
hygieneScenes.caption: No new contact. No new contamination assumed.
hygieneScenes.feedback: In this specific scenario, the hand hygiene action just completed already meets Moment 1. Do not automatically repeat it without a new indication. Reassess if you touch something or the task changes.

sbarParts.name: Situation
sbarParts.text: I am the practitioner caring for this fictional patient. They have a new clinical change and need prompt review.

sbarParts.name: Background
sbarParts.text: They were transferred to our care earlier today. The change is new compared with their documented baseline.

sbarParts.name: Assessment
sbarParts.text: My observations have changed from baseline. I am concerned about deterioration and need clinical support.

sbarParts.name: Recommendation
sbarParts.text: Please arrange an appropriate review now and confirm who will attend and the immediate plan.

chest.title: Seated chest opening
chest.description: A gentle seated demonstration of opening across the chest. Stay within a comfortable range.
steps: Sit upright on a stable, armless chair, away from the backrest. Keep both feet supported.
Bring your shoulders gently back and down; extend your arms to the sides without forcing them.
Gently bring the chest forward and up. The NHS example holds for 5–10 seconds.
Return with control. Keep breathing normally; stop rather than push into pain.
chest.sourceNote: NHS guidance describes a 5–10 second hold and 5 repetitions. This player is an illustrative preview, not a prescribed routine.

march.title: Seated hip marching
march.description: Alternate a comfortable lift of each bent knee while keeping your trunk steady.
steps: Sit upright, away from the back of a stable chair. Hold the sides of the seat.
Lift one bent knee only as far as comfortable. Avoid leaning back to make the lift larger.
Lower the foot with control and settle it on the floor.
Repeat with the opposite leg. Keep the range small if that is more comfortable.
phases: Settle upright and hold the seat
Lift and lower one bent knee
Return the foot to the floor
Lift and lower the other knee
march.sourceNote: NHS guidance describes 5 lifts per leg. One illustrated loop here includes both legs; the loop counter does not count your movement.

ankle.title: Seated ankle point & flex
ankle.description: With one leg gently extended, point the toes away and draw them back within a comfortable range.
steps: Sit upright on a stable chair and hold the sides of the seat.
Straighten one leg with the foot off the floor, only if comfortable.
Point your toes away, then gently draw them back towards you. Keep the movement at the ankle.
Return with control, then use the other leg when comfortable. This illustration shows one side.
phases: Settle upright and hold the seat
ankle.sourceNote: NHS guidance describes 2 sets of 5 stretches for each foot. The illustration shows one side only; no routine is prescribed by this app.

communication.situation: A fictional patient nods during an explanation but asks the same question again.
communication.poor: You understand now, right? The leaflet explains the rest.
communication.good: I have shared a lot. To check that I explained it clearly, how would you describe the next step in your own words?
why: A yes/no question can hide uncertainty.
The stronger version makes clarity the practitioner’s responsibility.
Use an interpreter or accessible format when needed.

safety.situation: A transfer list and a fictional patient’s account disagree about a medicine.
safety.poor: This list is newer, so I will use it and leave a note.
safety.good: These accounts differ. I will clarify the discrepancy with the responsible prescriber or pharmacist through the approved process before proceeding.
why: Recency alone does not establish correctness.
Documentation does not replace resolving a discrepancy.
The next team needs the verified plan.
safety.action: Name and clarify an uncertainty before acting.

empathy.situation: A fictional patient says an agreed follow-up plan will be difficult.
empathy.poor: You need to prioritize your health and make it work.
empathy.good: What would make this plan difficult to follow? Let us understand the barrier before we agree on the next step.
why: Advice can miss cost, transport, caring responsibilities, or understanding.
A curious question invites a useful explanation.
Adaptation belongs with the appropriate care team.
empathy.action: Ask one curious question before giving more advice.

sbar.situation: During a fictional handover, the receiving colleague does not know who will arrange a review.
sbar.poor: The patient needs checking. I mentioned it earlier, so someone should follow it up.
sbar.good: The review plan is still unclear. Can we confirm who will arrange the review, the agreed timing, and what we will do if that plan is not carried out?
why: The weak version transfers information without clear ownership.
A specific request makes the next action explicit.
Urgent deterioration needs the local escalation pathway immediately.
sbar.action: Confirm an owner, timing, and contingency at handover.

infection.situation: Shared equipment is about to move from one fictional patient area to another.
infection.poor: It looks clean, and neither patient is known to have an infection.
infection.good: I will follow the approved cleaning or reprocessing process before this equipment is used again, alongside the hand hygiene and precautions appropriate to the task.
why: Appearance does not establish that equipment is ready for reuse.
Standard precautions apply to all patient care.
Follow the equipment instructions and local process.
infection.action: Clarify who prepares shared equipment for the next use.

reasoning.situation: A colleague’s first explanation does not account for new information in a fictional case.
reasoning.poor: The first explanation still sounds likely. I will wait for more convincing evidence.
reasoning.good: This new finding does not fit our current explanation. What else should we consider, and who needs to review the mismatch now?
why: New information deserves reassessment.
Distinguish observed findings from interpretation.
Seek help through the appropriate route and within your scope.
reasoning.action: Ask what does not fit the initial explanation.

speakup.situation: A junior colleague questions an assumption during a fictional team discussion.
speakup.poor: We have already considered that. Let us keep moving.
speakup.good: Thank you for raising it. Tell us what you have noticed so we can check the concern and agree on the next step.
why: A dismissive response can discourage the next concern.
Invite observable details rather than debating status.
Urgent risks still require immediate escalation.
speakup.action: Thank the next person who raises a concern.

shared.situation: A fictional patient has two reasonable options with different practical burdens.
shared.poor: Most people choose option A. It is probably the easiest decision.
shared.good: Let us compare the benefits, harms, uncertainties, and practical demands of each option. What matters most to you in making this choice?
why: A common choice may not match the individual’s priorities.
Use balanced information and current decision support.
Check understanding and involve the responsible clinician.
shared.action: Ask what matters most before closing a decision.

ai.situation: A fictional AI summary offers a confident recommendation with an unfamiliar reference.
ai.poor: It includes a citation and the wording is clear, so it is ready to use.
ai.good: I will locate the actual source, check what it supports, and use the approved review process before relying on this claim.
why: A citation may be inaccurate or fabricated.
Asking the same tool for reassurance is not independent verification.
Keep confidential material out of unapproved tools.
ai.action: Independently verify one claim and its actual source.

wellbeing.situation: A fictional colleague reports persistent fatigue affecting concentration.
wellbeing.poor: Try a short breathing exercise and push through the rest of the week.
wellbeing.good: A brief pause may help now. Let us also discuss support and workload concerns through the appropriate supervisor or occupational-health route.
why: A short exercise does not address persistent strain on its own.
Working conditions and organizational support matter.
Seek qualified support for persistent or concerning symptoms.

equity.situation: A fictional patient agrees to a plan but the team has not checked language or access needs.
equity.poor: Their family member can translate, and the standard leaflet should be enough.
equity.good: Which language and communication format work best for you? We can arrange qualified interpretation and explore practical barriers through our service.
why: Do not infer understanding from agreement.
Qualified interpretation supports communication.
Accessibility needs should shape the agreed plan.
equity.action: Ask about language and access needs without assumptions.

improvement.situation: A fictional team notices that handovers repeatedly omit ownership of pending tasks.
improvement.poor: Remind everyone to be more careful and replace the whole form next week.
improvement.good: With the team and appropriate approval, test a small ownership prompt. Define how we will measure omissions and added burden before deciding whether to adapt it.
why: A reminder alone may leave the process unchanged.
A limited test makes learning manageable.
Check intended effects and unintended burden.
improvement.action: Define one small test and a measure before trying it.

health-literacy.situation: A fictional appointment message lists several unfamiliar abbreviations.
health-literacy.poor: The instructions are standard; please read them again.
health-literacy.good: Let us put this into everyday words and identify your next step together.
why: An explanation succeeds when the person can use it.
Prioritise what the person needs to do next. Use everyday words, a short written summary and accessible formats. Ask about language and communication preferences.
health-literacy.action: Ask a person to explain the next step after one short explanation.

risk-evidence.situation: A fictional flyer says an intervention halves an outcome.
risk-evidence.poor: A 50% reduction means 50 fewer people in every 100.
risk-evidence.good: What were the starting and ending risks, time period and population?
why: Always ask: compared with what, among whom, and over how long?
In a fictional example, an outcome falls from 4 in 100 to 2 in 100. That is 2 percentage points less, and a 50% relative reduction. These describe the same change in different ways.
risk-evidence.action: Check the absolute figures behind one relative-risk claim.

human-factors.situation: A fictional team misses a task after repeated interruptions.
human-factors.good: Let us map the interruption and test a visible task cue with a named owner.
why: A reliable process supports people when attention and memory are stretched.
Reduce unnecessary complexity. Use a visible task owner, a clear cue or an approved checklist at the point of work. A reminder to concentrate is a weak response to a recurring design problem.
human-factors.action: Map one fragile step with the people who perform it.

med-transitions.situation: Two fictional lists disagree about whether Medicine A is current.
med-transitions.poor: The newest list must be right.
med-transitions.good: The accounts conflict. I will seek verification through the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
why: A discrepancy is a question to resolve, not an instruction to guess.
Record the uncertainty and route it to the responsible clinician or pharmacist. Do not decide to start, stop or change a medicine from this learning exercise.
med-transitions.action: Clarify ownership of a reconciliation question.

deterioration.situation: A fictional record says stable but new information is concerning.
deterioration.poor: The earlier note was reassuring, so I will wait.
deterioration.good: There is a new change and I am concerned. I will activate the appropriate local response now.
why: Communicate significant concern before certainty arrives.
For urgent concern, use the local emergency or escalation pathway immediately. A communication mnemonic must not become a waiting sequence or substitute for clinical assessment.
deterioration.action: Review where to find your local escalation pathway.

data-stewardship.situation: A fictional note without a name is proposed for a public tool.
data-stewardship.poor: No name means no privacy concern.
data-stewardship.good: Other details may identify the person; we need an approved workflow before sharing.
why: Useful information still needs an authorised purpose and destination.
Names are not the only identifiers. Dates, locations, rare details and combinations can identify someone. Removing a name alone does not establish anonymity.
data-stewardship.action: Identify the approved information-governance contact for your setting.

teachback-skill.situation: A fictional patient explains a follow-up plan differently.
teachback-skill.good: Thank you. I need to explain that part more clearly. Let us try it another way.
why: Teach-back is a loop, not a yes/no question.
Say: To check that I explained it clearly, how would you describe what happens next? Frame the check around your explanation.
teachback-skill.action: Rehearse one repair phrase with a colleague.

conflict.situation: A fictional handover lacks a named task owner.
conflict.good: This task has no named owner. Can we agree who will act and when?
why: A useful disagreement ends with a clearer next action.
Ask for the other perspective and name the common aim. Explore constraints without assuming that disagreement reflects poor intent.
conflict.action: Rephrase one accusation as an observation and request.

documentation.situation: A fictional note reads: team aware, follow up later.
documentation.good: I will record the agreed action, named owner, timing and any outstanding question in the approved record.
why: A record should make the next action easier to understand.
Include the agreed action, responsible person, timing and unresolved questions according to your local documentation requirements.
documentation.action: Check one fictional note for a missing owner or time.

risk-dialogue.situation: A fictional option reduces an outcome from 10 in 100 to 8 in 100.
risk-dialogue.poor: It cuts the risk by 20%, so it is clearly best.
risk-dialogue.good: In this example that is 2 fewer people in 100 over the same period. Let us compare burdens and uncertainty too.
why: Balanced numbers support a decision; they do not choose it for the person.
Invite the person to describe their interpretation. A visual display can support a conversation, but it does not replace accessible explanation.

feedback.situation: In a fictional rehearsal, ownership was omitted at handover.
feedback.good: The action owner was missing. How did you see that moment, and could we practise an explicit closing request?
why: Useful feedback gives someone something specific they can try.
Describe an observable behaviour and its effect. Ask how the other person saw the situation before offering a conclusion. Avoid labels about character.
feedback.action: Give one specific observation and invite a response.

debrief.situation: A fictional team finishes a challenging practice session.
debrief.poor: We finished, so there is nothing to discuss.
debrief.good: What helped, what was difficult, and which one change will we review next time?
why: A debrief needs both curiosity and follow-through.
Ask what was expected, what happened, what helped and what made the task difficult. Invite different roles and distinguish facts from assumptions.
debrief.action: Close a debrief with one named learning action.

humility.situation: New information challenges a fictional team’s first view.
humility.good: This does not fit our earlier view. What should we reconsider and who needs to review it?
why: Changing your mind can be a sign of careful thinking.
Ask what does not fit and who may have another perspective. A patient, caregiver or colleague may notice something missing from the current account.
humility.action: Ask what information would change an assumption.

dignity.situation: A fictional discussion addresses a companion while the patient is present.
dignity.good: I would like to hear from you directly. What support would make this discussion easier?
why: Respect is expressed through permission, privacy and participation.
Explain your role and the intended conversation or task. Ask permission within the applicable consent process, protect privacy and respect the person’s questions.
dignity.action: Ask a communication preference before assuming one.

just-culture.situation: A fictional team discovers a near miss.
just-culture.poor: Find the person responsible and close the issue.
just-culture.good: Let us establish the facts, follow the reporting process and understand the conditions fairly.
why: Fairness needs both context and accountability.
Ask about workload, tools, interruptions, unclear responsibilities and other influences. A systems approach does not mean ignoring deliberate unsafe behaviour or professional obligations.
just-culture.action: Ask how the process made the error possible.

accountability.situation: A fictional colleague assumes someone will arrange a review.
accountability.good: Let us confirm who owns the action, by when, and what happens if they cannot complete it.
why: Accountability includes saying when a task needs help.
If a commitment cannot be met, communicate the constraint early through the appropriate route. Agree an alternative owner or contingency rather than allowing a silent gap.
accountability.action: Close one handover with named responsibility.

compassion-boundaries.situation: A fictional colleague is struggling with continuing workload.
compassion-boundaries.poor: A quick breathing exercise will fix it.
compassion-boundaries.good: I can listen and help identify support. We should also raise the workload concern through the appropriate route.
why: Compassion can be warm, practical and honest about limits.
Explain what you can help with and what needs a different service or professional. Clear boundaries can make support more reliable.
compassion-boundaries.action: Identify one realistic support action and one limit.

inclusive-leadership.situation: A fictional meeting repeatedly hears only its most senior members.
inclusive-leadership.good: Which perspective have we not heard, and what other way to contribute would help?
why: An invitation matters more when people can see how it was used.
Offer accessible materials and appropriate ways to contribute before, during or after the discussion. Invite concerns without putting someone on display.
inclusive-leadership.action: Offer a second accessible route for input.

Simplicity matters but is only one part of a balanced discussion.
Others’ choices cannot establish this person’s values or needs.
Balanced evidence, uncertainty, and personal priorities belong in the same discussion.

Independent source checking tests both the reference and the claim.
More detail from the same system can repeat or elaborate an error.
Agreement between generated answers is not independent verification.

Suggest a quiet break and review how they feel at the next shift.
Offer immediate support and discuss workload through the proper route.
Share self-care resources and ask them to choose one to practise.
A break may help now, but waiting can leave ongoing safety and workload concerns unaddressed.
Immediate support and attention to working conditions address more than individual coping.
Resources can help, but should not replace practical support and organizational responsibility.
equity: A fictional patient agrees to a plan, but language and access needs have not been explored. What is the best next step?
Offer the standard leaflet and invite the family to explain it.
Ask whether the patient is comfortable continuing in this language.
Ask about preferred communication support and practical access needs.
A standard leaflet and family explanation may not meet the person’s communication needs.
This opens the discussion but can still miss format, interpretation, and practical barriers.
A direct, respectful needs check supports an accessible and workable plan.
improvement: A fictional team wants to reduce missing task owners at handover. Which next step supports learning from a small test?
Agree a limited change, a measure, and a check for added burden.
Introduce an ownership field across the service and gather comments.
Repeat the handover training and count how many staff attend.
A defined test, measure, and balancing check make the result interpretable.
A wider change can create avoidable disruption before a small test has generated learning.
Attendance is an activity measure; it does not show whether missing ownership improved.

harm.title: Preventable harm across care settings
harm.finding: Preventable harm was reported across multiple care settings.
harm.population: 70 observational studies; 337,025 patients across medical care settings.
harm.context: Pooled estimate 6% (95% CI 5–7%). Rates and definitions varied between studies. This is historical synthesis, not a local incident rate or Carecraft outcome.

handoff.title: A structured handoff programme
numbers: relative reduction in preventable adverse events
handoff.finding: Error rates fell after implementation of the I-PASS bundle.
handoff.population: Nine paediatric residency programmes; 10,740 patient admissions.
handoff.context: A multicomponent intervention, not an SBAR-only effect. Before-and-after associations do not isolate every cause or predict this app’s effect.

medication.title: Medication reconciliation at transitions
numbers: discrepancies per patient at the start
discrepancies per patient at the end
medication.source: Schnipper et al. · BMJ Quality & Safety · 2022
medication.finding: Discrepancy rates fell during the MARQUIS2 implementation.
medication.population: 18 North American hospitals or hospital systems, with data collection at 17; 2016–2018.
medication.context: Observed rates across an 18-month, mentored, multicomponent intervention. A discrepancy is not synonymous with injury. No individual tool effect or dose decision is inferred.

ipc.title: A bundle for catheter-related infection
ipc.finding: A coordinated infection-prevention programme was associated with sustained improvement.
ipc.population: Michigan intensive-care units; catheter-related bloodstream infections; 18-month study.
ipc.context: Historical, multicomponent ICU programme. This is not the effect of hand hygiene alone, a general infection rate, or proof that a Studio prevents infections.

access.title: Accessibility is a routine need
numbers: of US adults reported functional disability
access.source: CDC · Disability and Health Data Now · 2025
access.finding: Accessible services matter to a substantial part of the adult population.
access.population: 2022 US Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, reported by CDC.
access.context: US self-reported survey data, not global or Saudi prevalence. Definitions differ from other surveys. The figure does not reveal any individual’s needs: ask the person.

wellbeing.title: Burnout and reported safety incidents
wellbeing.finding: Physician burnout was associated with higher odds of safety incidents.
wellbeing.population: 239,246 physicians in the full review. The overall-burnout/safety analysis used 35 studies and 41,059 physicians.
wellbeing.context: OR 2.04 (95% CI 1.69–2.45); substantial heterogeneity. Odds are not risk. Association does not establish causation or the effect of an individual wellbeing exercise.

engagement.title: Decision aids improve understanding
engagement.finding: Decision aids improved knowledge compared with usual care.
engagement.population: 107,698 adults in the full review. The knowledge estimate pooled 107 studies and 25,492 participants.
engagement.context: Mean difference 11.90/100 (95% CI 10.60–13.19), high-certainty evidence for this outcome. Evidence searched to March 2022; aids supplement clinical consultation.

teachback.title: Teach-back across different settings
numbers: reported benefit on at least one outcome
teachback.finding: Teach-back showed promising results, with varied methods and outcomes.
teachback.population: Studies across different populations and care settings, searched to July 2019.
teachback.context: Counts of studies, not a 95% treatment benefit. Seven studies were rated weak and outcomes were heterogeneous; no single pooled clinical effect is claimed.

empathy.title: Empathy and positive communication
empathy.source: Howick et al. · Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine · 2018
empathy.finding: The empathy subgroup found a small improvement in pooled patient outcomes.
empathy.population: Seven trials tested empathic consultations; other trials tested positive expectations.
empathy.context: Empathy subgroup SMD −0.18 (95% CI −0.32 to −0.03). This standardised effect is not a percentage reduction. Conditions, outcomes and certainty varied.

interruptions.title: Interruptions during medication work
interruptions.source: Westbrook et al. · Archives of Internal Medicine · 2010
interruptions.finding: More interruptions were associated with more errors in the observed setting.
interruptions.population: 98 nurses, six wards, two Sydney teaching hospitals; 2006–2008 observations.
interruptions.context: Each interruption was associated with a 12.7% increase in clinical errors in the study model. Observational association, not a universal error probability or a rationale to delay urgent communication.

digital.title: A citation can look real and still be false
numbers: fabricated citations in the GPT-3.5 sample
fabricated citations in the GPT-4 sample
digital.finding: The sampled outputs contained fabricated and erroneous references.
digital.population: 636 citations generated for the study’s prompts using 2023-era models.
digital.context: Historical benchmark, not a current error rate for all AI systems or clinical outputs. Different prompts, versions and verification workflows can produce different results.

simulation.title: Why actively rehearse?
simulation.finding: Simulation training outperformed no intervention on pooled learning outcomes.
simulation.population: Multiple health professions and simulation formats; 137 randomised studies plus other designs.
simulation.context: Large heterogeneity and predominantly pre/post studies. The comparison was no intervention; it does not establish superiority to every teaching method or validate these particular simulations.

audit.title: Feedback can support better practice
audit.finding: Audit and feedback improved desired professional practice on average.
audit.population: The mean estimate pooled 177 studies comparing audit and feedback with control.
audit.context: 95% CI 4.1–8.2 percentage points; moderate-certainty evidence. Effects varied and interventions often included education or reminders. This is not an effect of informal feedback alone.

zones.question: What remains to be agreed?
answers: That the message was long enough.
Who will act, the agreed timing and how responsibility is accepted.
That everyone in the room has received a copy.
why: Length does not establish ownership.
An explicit owner and timing turn acknowledgment into an actionable plan.
More recipients can still leave responsibility unassigned.

zones.name: The communication station
zones.label: Close
zones.copy: A named person has accepted the action. The fictional team has not agreed what happens if the review is delayed or the situation changes.
zones.question: Which closing action is useful?
answers: Assume the original plan will happen.
Document the concern and end the discussion.
Confirm the contingency and local re-escalation route, alongside the approved record.
why: A plan also needs a response to delay or change.
Documentation supports communication but does not establish the contingency.
Closing the loop includes what to do when the plan cannot be carried out.

CC_SIMS.title: The interruption recovery desk
CC_SIMS.description: Inspect a task desk, distinguish competing demands and recover a verified task state.
CC_SIMS.why: An interruption can leave task status, urgency and ownership uncertain.
CC_SIMS.when: When reviewing interruption-prone work or planning a safer task handoff.
CC_SIMS.how: Inspect the task record, incoming demand and return point. Choose a response at each hotspot.

zones.name: The task record
zones.label: Verify
zones.copy: A fictional coordination task was interrupted. A checklist is open, but you do not remember which parts were completed. This is a communication exercise, not medication preparation.
zones.question: What is the useful starting point?
answers: Resume where you think you were.
Check the approved task record and establish completed and outstanding steps.
Mark the task complete to prevent duplication.
why: Memory alone may not reveal the actual task state.
A verified task state is a stronger basis for resuming than an assumption.
Unverified completion can hide outstanding work.

zones.name: The incoming demand
zones.label: Prioritise
zones.copy: A colleague interrupts with a request. The scenario does not establish whether the request is urgent. “Never interrupt” would be an unsafe blanket rule.
zones.question: What should you clarify?
answers: The request’s urgency and appropriate response, using local escalation where indicated.
Whether the colleague can wait in every circumstance.
Whether ignoring requests will make the queue smaller.
why: Urgent concerns must not be blocked by a task-protection habit. Clarify the actual need.
Some requests require immediate attention.
Silence does not resolve urgency or responsibility.

zones.name: The return tray
zones.label: Resume
zones.copy: You have addressed the incoming demand. A second person may have moved the original task forward while you were away.
zones.question: How do you avoid a silent gap or duplicate work?
answers: Restart every step regardless of what others did.
Continue from the original memory of your place.
Confirm the current status and owner, then resume from the verified point.
why: A full restart may introduce unnecessary duplication; first establish the state.
The task may have changed while you were away.
A status-and-ownership check supports a deliberate return.

CC_SIMS.title: The shared-choice consultation
CC_SIMS.description: Explore a consultation space, compare fictional numbers and bring the person’s priorities into the plan.
CC_SIMS.why: A balanced comparison needs evidence, uncertainty and the person’s practical priorities.
CC_SIMS.when: Before rehearsing a shared-decision or risk-explanation conversation.
CC_SIMS.how: Explore the person’s priorities, the number board and the follow-up plan. The displayed numbers are synthetic.

zones.name: The person’s priorities
zones.label: Ask
zones.copy: In a fictional conversation, two possible plans have different visit and preparation burdens. The person has not been asked what would be difficult or important to them.
zones.question: Which question makes the comparison more useful?
answers: Which plan does the team prefer?
What matters most to you, and what would make either plan difficult?
Which option is most popular?
why: Team preference alone does not establish the person’s priorities.
A preference-and-barrier question helps connect options to the individual.
A popular option may not fit this person.

zones.name: The fictional number board
zones.label: Compare
zones.copy: Synthetic example: the same outcome occurs in 8 of 100 people with one option and 5 of 100 with another, over the same period. No treatment, real-world rate or causal claim is implied.
zones.question: Which explanation keeps the absolute difference visible?
answers: That is 3 fewer in 100, or 3 percentage points, alongside burdens and uncertainty.
That is 37.5 fewer people in every 100.
The second option guarantees a better outcome for this person.
why: 8/100 minus 5/100 is 3/100. The baseline, time period and trade-offs remain important.
37.5% is the relative reduction in this synthetic example, not the absolute number in 100.
A group-level probability does not guarantee an individual result.

zones.name: The shared next step
zones.label: Agree
zones.copy: The person wants time to consider the options and discuss a practical barrier. The plan is not yet agreed.
zones.question: What supports an informed next step?
answers: Record agreement because the information has been provided.
Choose the option with the larger-looking percentage.
Clarify the support needed and agree appropriate follow-up with the responsible clinician.
why: Receiving information is not the same as reaching a shared agreement.
A percentage alone cannot resolve priorities and uncertainty.
Support, ownership and follow-up help the decision remain informed and revisable.
